metadata.file_name: 156. Veletić & Olsen (2024). Exploring school leadership profiles across the world  a cluster analysis approach to TALIS 2018.pdf
metadata.title: Exploring school leadership profiles across the world: a cluster analysis approach to TALIS 2018
metadata.venue: International Journal of Leadership in Education

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 school- and teacher-level data collected via a two-stage sampling design (random sample of schools within each country, then random sample of teachers within schools). Prior to clustering, the authors standardized the 12 leadership-for-learning scales using “senate weights” so that all countries contribute equally to the scale metric. Factor scores for the TALIS scales were calculated using Mplus with TYPE = COMPLEX and school weights to account for non-independence and unequal probability of selection. For the clustering stage, the paper does not report additional explicit application of student/school sampling weights beyond the earlier standardization and the use of senate weights for equal country contribution.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the dependent variables are leadership-for-learning scale factor scores (and one derived factor score) used for descriptive clustering, not cognitive achievement outcomes with PVs. The paper also does not report any PV-based achievement modeling; instead, it uses standardized scale scores and then applies k-means clustering to form school leadership profiles.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis uses TALIS 2018 core survey data for lower secondary education (ISCED Level 2) from 48 participating countries/economies. The study reports a total of 7,427 schools from 43 countries after excluding six countries due to systematically missing school-level data (Argentina, Iceland, Japan, Sweden, Denmark, Hungary). For the remaining sample, listwise deletion was applied, with the authors noting that the listwise-deletion effect varied by country (0.68% to 35.94%, average 11.86%). Additionally, for cluster validation, schools with negative silhouette coefficients were excluded from further analyses to purify the cluster solution.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Best model: Decision Tree (see outcome_summary for metrics)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Primary analytic outcome (inferred from extraction), finding that This study uses TALIS 2018 (lower secondary; teachers and principals) to construct leadership-for-learning profiles across schools and to examine whether country-level groupings emerge. The authors mapped TALIS 2018 questionnaire scales onto an eight-dimension Leadership for Learning framework and used 12 leadership scale factor scores (six principal, six teacher) as indicators; one principal scale (instructional autonomy) was derived for the study. After standardizing scales using senate weights, they aggregated teacher variables to the school level and applied k-means clustering, selecting k=5 via elbow and silhouette methods. Variance decomposition showed that most variability lay between schools rather than between countries, leading to a school-level clustering solution. The five-cluster solution accounted for 25.9% of variability in school profiles; 790 schools (15%) had negative silhouette coefficients, and the authors excluded these for cluster purification. The study reports that country-level cluster membership does not align with geographic/linguistic/political proximity, while leadership profiles are present in most countries and show teacher–principal perception gaps in distributed leadership. data.null_fields_interpretation: The paper is an exploratory clustering study rather than a supervised predictive ML study, so there are no target variables with predictive performance metrics to extract into main_findings. Consequently, plausible-values handling is not applicable (the outcomes are leadership scale factor scores used for descriptive profiling), and confounders_identified is empty because the clustering inputs are not treated as ML predictors with a causal/predictive target.
